The Problem: 
Ill-equipped leaders are lending to toxic workplaces, climates, and cultures.  
 
The Way Forward: 
Encourage self-awareness towards self-leadership and development. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
© 2023 | Maribel Paulino 
ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.  
 
Abstract:   
Toxic workplaces are recognized as the strongest predictor of attrition and turnover, 
contributing to global disengagement (70% of team engagement is attributed to managers who 
are also quietly quitting) particularly by way of workplace cultures, pay and benefits, and 
employee well-being. A recent workplace research study suggests that 59% of the global 
workforce is disengaged, 44% is experiencing record high stress levels, 21% is experiencing 
anger, 56% is struggling, and 24% feel cared for; meanwhile, global disengagement is costing 
the global economy a substantial $8.8 trillion dollars. As the world continues to evolve, leaders 
must forge ahead continuously shifting how they lead, and self-lead, to effectively manage 
themselves and talent. Leaders need to align themselves, as well as the right resources, to 
organizational values and purpose in hopes to circumvent contributing to the increasing attrition 
rates, and refrain from compromising and unethical leadership behaviors.  
To lead effectively, leaders must become architects of their own experiences and 
overcome obstacles rooted in personal fears, ego, and unproductive habits. Hence, self-leading, 
via self-awareness, is foundational before one can teach or lead. More importantly, as change 
agents called to compassionately influence and shift cultures, leaders are afforded a 
transformative opportunity to rise tides, creating ripple effects conducive for the lifting of all 
surrounding boats. However, impactful waves of transformation can only be achieved when 
focused on steering one’s own boat and leading oneself, first, before leading others. As such, this 
thesis will explore leading via the concepts of courage, self-awareness, and communication to 
encourage self-analysis for the cultivation of individual self-leadership cultures towards effective 
organizational outcomes. It proposes self-leadership to address relationship based workplace 
challenges, such as toxic cultures and quiet quitting, by leveraging effective communication 
practices, behavior change models, theories of motivation, and the cultivation of positive 
climates, cultures, and psychological safety. 
 Keywords: Courage, Leadership Communication, Power, Psychological Safety, Self-
Awareness, Self-Leadership, Trust, Toxic Workplace Climates & Cultures   
 
Why Self-Leadership, Why Now 
Congratulations, you have been hired are often words shouted at the mountain tops that at 
a first glance can appear to be glorious until surrounding voices begin to question hiring 
decisions made. Leaders, including Human Resource leads, have the immense task of 
appropriately taking calculated risks when considering new hires, transfers, retention strategies, 
and high potentials. Instrumental to directing energies, leadership needs to ensure to hire the 
right people aligned to organizational values and purpose; people who are agile, adaptable, and 
resilient to remain focused and in the game. They must have the capacity to pivot when 
necessary, requiring active listening, a sense of curiosity, less ego, and managed insecurities to 
circumvent compromising and unethical leadership behaviors. 
Brown, Sull, & Sull (2022) suggest that “toxic organizational cultures are the strongest 
predictor of attrition and turnover, and are, to no surprise, 10x more important than 
compensation.” A recent workplace research study demonstrates the undeniable impact of toxic 
cultures as 2022 was marked by record high stress levels impacting productivity, well-being, and 
performance (Gallup, 2023, p. 5). The research suggests that 59% of the global workforce was 
disengaged (quietly quitted) predominantly due to workplace culture (41%; followed by pay and 
benefits (28%) and well-being (16%)) and 44% experienced high stress levels (followed by anger 
(21%)), which also negatively influences engagement (Gallup, 2023, pp. 4-12). Gallup (2023, p. 
11) suggests that “70% of team engagement is attributable to managers; however, managers, too, 
are quietly quitting due to an absence of appropriate team building tools (skills);” so, who is 
leading whom? 
Furthermore, they suggest that 56% of the global workforce is struggling and 24% feel 
their organization cares (Gallup, n.d.); meanwhile, disengagement costs continue to negatively 
impact the global economy ($8.8 trillion accounting for 9% of the global GDP) (Gallup, 2023, p. 
 
4). For those who think emotions don’t belong at work, Clifton (Gallup, 2023, p. 1) believes that 
poor management not only leads to lost talent, customers, and profits, but it also produces 
negative emotions that impact an employee’s overall well-being, unfavorably impacting both 
personal and professional spaces. However, according to Gallup (2023, pp. 4-13), 
disengagement, reframed, can offer leaders an opportunity to reconvert employees by inspiring 
and encouraging quiet quitters to become productive via effective coaching tactics. 
Leadership is all about influencing, creating impact, driving direction, setting the tone, 
providing encouragement, and serving others, which can only effectively be done when we are 
first honest with ourselves. Leading requires one to go first, ensuring to lead oneself and serve as 
an example as the most authentic form of leadership begins with how you lead you. Hence, this 
thesis will explore leading via the concepts of courage, self-awareness, and communication to 
encourage self-analysis for the cultivation of individual self-leadership cultures. It proposes self-
leadership to address relationship-based workplace challenges, such as toxic cultures and quiet 
quitting, by leveraging effective communication practices, behavior change models, theories of 
motivation, and the cultivation of positive climates, cultures, and psychological safety. 
If there is anything that society has learned is that a lack of preparedness is detrimental to 
one’s success. The COVID-19 pandemic, in particular, has brought about a mental health 
awareness movement to the forefront, infectiously injecting fear into organizational cultures. 
“Fear has led to the slow downfall and collapse of organizations from the inside out,” 
contributing to quiet quitting, re-evaluations (aka the great resignation era), and the deployment 
of crisis management strategies (Rieger, 2011, para. 2). When leaders are ill-equipped, a lack of 
self-awareness exacerbates how a crisis is managed, or mismanaged, leading to increased 
negative ripple effects across an organization. Consequently, ineffective and unchecked 
 
leadership will eventually seep into and affect the atmosphere. McKeon (2023) said it best when 
he stated that “a toxic workplace can be like a toxic relationship as it takes courage to break 
away due to fear, threats, manipulation, and gaslighting.” Hence, “to overcome various fears (ie.: 
failure, a loss of budget, headcount, or respect) one must implement a culture of courage (by: 1) 
aligning courage, 2) matching strengths with responsibilities, 3) engaging employees, and 4) 
rewarding courageous behaviors)” and shift from the unknown to the known which requires a 
level of organizational and individual self-awareness (Rieger, 2011, para. 4). 
Leading in uncertainty will require the identification of where you are, and where you 
want to be, to then determine how best to get there. As a prerequisite to engagement, Rieger 
(2011, para. 19) suggests that both vital and moral courage (see differences in exhibit 1) are 
required to combat fear-based organizational barriers, which inhibit engagement, as a company 
can have various cultures within individual workgroups. Rieger (2011, para. 17) believes that 
organizations will never overcome fear-based obstacles while pinning employees against 
themselves (forcing employees to choose between what’s best for themselves or the 
organization). However, there is a delicate balance to be managed when finding one’s voice, 
rooted in confidence, ensuring not to lower one’s standards to do so. It is the greatest expression 
of leadership and self-love, and requires great courage, self-awareness, effective communication, 
and self-leadership. 
Leading via Courage, Self-Awareness, & Effective Communication 
Courage Relative to Leadership 
"The only way to happiness is freedom, and the only way to freedom is courage."  
~ Epictetus, Stoic Greek Philosopher ~ 
Courage as defined by the Merriam-Webster (n.d.) dictionary refers to one's mental or 
 
moral strength to persevere and withstand times of difficulty, danger, or pain. It is a quality of 
mind (or mindset) and spirit to act in accordance with one’s values and beliefs, while courageous 
behavior (or bravery; see exhibit 2 for a list of behaviors that require courage) refers to the act 
of showing courage. Courage, in turn, provides the necessary strength for resiliency to help one 
bounce forward towards adaptability during challenging times (De Smet, Kothari, & Lavoie, 
2021, p. 2).  
Brown (n.d., para. 1) suggests that “leadership is not about titles, but rather is a 
willingness to compassionately lean into courage,” enabling authentic connections. Feser et al’s 
(2019, p. 2) leadership perspective (as a set of leadership behaviors) highlights the importance of 
courageous leadership for authentic relationship building. As such, courage is recognized as the 
glue that reinforces accountability, commitment, self-discipline, deliberate choices and 
behaviors, and intentional actions. It impacts workplace performance and career advancement, 
and has the potential to “thwart learning and growth when unproductive or bad behaviors are 
inadvertently encouraged, rewarded, or modeled” (Detert & Bruno, 2021, p. 4).  
Workplace courage is required for effective problem solving, decision making, pushing 
appropriate agendas, influencing and shaping decisions, as well as championing new initiatives 
(Detert & Bruno, 2021, p. 3). However, Detert (2021, para. 3) also warns of the dangers of 
encouraging courageous behaviors in psychologically unsafe environments. He believes that, as 
leaders, “to tell the people below you to be more courageous without changing risky behaviors 
and conditions, is to displace responsibility onto people with less power” (Detert, 2021, para. 3). 
De Smet et al (2021, p. 4) agree as they believe that challenging negative behaviors will not have 
a positive effect in the absence of a positive foundational workplace climate. 
The notion of ‘displaced responsibility’ brings to mind Abraham Maslow’s Hierarchy of 
 
Needs (see exhibit 3), where he introduces a motivational theory to help explain human 
hierarchical needs. His theory suggests that foundational needs are critical to the success of 
subsequent levels, which will only emerge when prior levels have been sufficiently satisfied. 
According to McLeod (2023, para. 5), these needs are divided into two distinct sets of needs: 
deficiency and growth or being needs.  
The first four levels (physiological, safety, love and belonging, and esteem) are 
considered physiological deficiencies or survival needs that lend to behaviors motivated by lack 
(McLeod, 2023, para. 5-7). Whereas the fifth level (self-actualization1) is considered a 
psychological growth need associated with reaching one's full potential (McLeod, 2023, para. 
12). When considering Maslow’s theory of needs within an organizational setting, McLeod 
(2023, para. 21) suggests that these needs are flexible and behaviors can be driven by differing 
and simultaneous needs. While the model has later been expanded (see exhibit 4), Maslow’s 
theory reconfirms the critical subjective nature of trust and highlights courage dependencies and 
self-actualizing behaviors, particularly when experiencing displaced leadership responsibility. 
Courage impacts a leader's capacity to manage, mobilize, and leverage effective decision 
making across an organization's vision through to fruition (analysis, strategy identification, 
implementation, end results) (Şen, Kabak, & Yangınlar, 2013, p. 96). At the core of leadership, 
courage is recognized as foundational to human values with the capacity to increase overall 
effectiveness (Şen, Kabak, & Yangınlar, 2013, p. 94). It impacts the leadership process (see 
exhibit 5) and affects key values such as honesty, integrity, equality, justice, and fairness 
amongst others (Şen, Kabak, & Yangınlar, 2013, p. 95). Interestingly enough, “the amount and 
depth of core courage characteristics (see exhibit 6: moral, creativity, biological, knowledge, 
 1 Self-Actualization: as the highest level in Maslow’s hierarchy, it “refers to the realization of a person’s potential, self-fulfillment, seeking personal growth, and peak experiences” (McLeod, 2023); a state of continual becoming. 
 
followers) determines the degree of courage possessed by a leader” (Şen, Kabak, & Yangınlar, 
2013, p. 95). Hence, the greater the courage characteristic level, the greater the capacity and 
display of behavior (Şen, Kabak, & Yangınlar, 2013, p. 95). Courage as well as courageous 
behavior are then dependent on satisfying foundational human needs as well as having a 
balanced level of courage characteristics. 
Susan David, psychologist and author of Emotional Agility, describes courage as fear 
walking (David, 2022- b, para. 9). In this light, in moments where one may feel stuck, hopeless, 
or powerless, calculated risks and efforts made to courageously move forward, despite fear, is 
one’s greatest reward and act of bravery. As one confronts personal or organizational fears, 
leaders must recognize that courage is built on three pillars of trust (empathy, logic, and 
authenticity) (Frei, 2018), and that followers reluctantly give their hands, but not their head or 
hearts, when uncommitted (Maxwell, 2011, p. 61). 
 Sucher & Gupta (2019, para. 62) further posit that the building of trust is dependent on 
having a “clear purpose, smart strategy, and a definitive action.” However, on the other hand, 
Arundhati Roy (2004), author of The God of Small Things, believes “there’s no such thing as the 
voiceless; there are only the deliberately silenced and the preferably unheard.” In hopes to 
address trust levels, leaders can cultivate a culture of psychological safety and appreciation by 
reframing failures and encouraging and amplifying team voices (De Smet, Kothari, & Lavoie, 
2021, p. 8). Thus, leaders must courageously predetermine the effect and impact they wish to 
have, wholeheartedly connecting with their ‘why’. 
Maxwell (2011, pp. 63-76) describes good leadership as one who leads with others 
(collaboratively, inclusively, selflessly) and is prepared to confront the uncomfortable nature of 
growth to earn followers enthusiasm, loyalty, and the devotion of hearts, minds, and souls. 
 
Maxwell (2011, pp. 79-80) believes defining one's leadership, shifting one’s focus from position 
to potential, as well as shifting one’s leadership approach from rules to relationships is where 
growth begins. The expression of courageous behavior requires a growth mindset coupled with a 
relational approach to enable connections and relationship building. It requires a balanced level 
of intellectual (what to do, how to do it, and why) and emotional (understanding why) knowledge 
(Şen, Kabak, & Yangınlar, 2013, p. 96) and confidence, rooted in grace and courage, to identify 
your core values as well as who you are. 
Unsuccessful transformations or behavior changes were found to be intricately linked to 
emotional, than intellectual, knowledge as employees often lack self-awareness (Keller & 
Schaninger, 2019, p. 5). Hence, De Smet, Kothari, & Lavoie (2021, p. 2) propose adaptability as 
the key for transformation and systemic changes to increase one’s learning capacity fostered via 
an adaptive mindset. Ironically, the paradox of adaptability is such that when confronted with 
challenges, one tends to lean towards the familiar, stifling growth and development (De Smet, 
Kothari, & Lavoie, 2021, p. 2). 
In this same lens, when considering Victor Frankl’s (author of Man's Search for 
Meaning) infamous behavior change equation (Stimulus(S) + Thinking(T) = Response(R)), 
leaning towards the unfamiliar requires having the appropriate mindset, rooted in self-trust 
(builds self-confidence and impacts one’s feelings (emotions)), to drive effective behavior 
change. Tkachenko et al (2018, p. 902) believe that courage is a crucial and virtuous predictor 
for executive performance and is associated with workplace satisfaction. They believe courage is 
about accountability and, therefore, also believe it is a leader’s responsibility to develop and 
facilitate behavioral courage (Tkachenko et al, 2018, p. 910). Courageous behavior requires a 
level of tactfulness conducive to successfully navigating difficult conversations and adding 
 
value. Consequently, courage drives the necessary self-awareness required for leadership 
effectiveness. 
The Imperative Nature of Self-Awareness  
Simon Sinek (2022), author and founder of the Optimism Company, stated it best when 
he said that “the ability to be vulnerable is one of the greatest (and most difficult) leadership 
lessons any of us can learn”; but how can anyone effectively lead and be of service with limited 
knowledge of self and while unaware? Despite universal monitoring, he suggests that 
“performance is not an accurate indicator of stress levels, and that vulnerability, instead, allows 
room for trust and human-centered leadership” (Sinek, 2022), introducing the critical need for 
self-awareness. 
Self-awareness as described by Executive Coach, Organizational Psychologist, 
Researcher, and Author, Tasha Eurich, is “not one singular truth” (Eurich, 2023), rather is a rare 
quality with two distinct, and at times, competing viewpoints (see exhibit 7 where she proposes 
four self-awareness archetypes): internal (one’s inner world) and external awareness (how one’s 
perceived by others) (Eurich, 2018, para. 7-12). She defines self-awareness as a delicate balance 
and capacity to see your own “values, passions, aspirations, environmental fit, reactions, and 
impact on others” (internal), and understand how one is perceived within those same parameters 
(external) (Eurich, 2018, para. 7). 
Eurich (2018, para. 7) believes that internal self-awareness is “positively associated with 
job satisfaction, personal and social control and happiness, and is negatively associated with 
anxiety, stress, and depression.” She believes that we become more “confident, creative, better 
decision makers, build stronger relationships, communicate more effectively, and are more 
effective leaders when we ‘see’ ourselves clearly” (Eurich, 2018, para. 1). Additionally, Eurich 
 
(2018, para. 19-21) suggests that introspection, when done correctly, can also serve as a tool to 
increase self-insight by leveraging ‘what’ questions towards a solution-orientation. 
Brassy, De Smet, & Kruyt (2023, p. 1) reframe the concept of ‘competing viewpoints’ as 
a “dual and integrated awareness that enables one to act intentionally and perform optimally 
despite circumstances or environments.” They suggest that there are “five levels of awareness 
(see exhibit 8) which require emotion and thought detachment to create room for self-
observation, positioning one with the opportunity to choose how best to respond” (pp. 1-2). 
Emotions are data points that enable one to appropriately pivot, indicating a need for self-
examination to effectively frame, and reframe, directions and approaches (David, 2022-a, para. 
2-5). David (2022-a, para. 7) believes that “recognizing the influence of one’s emotions can also 
help guide one toward productive outcomes.” This awareness allows one to overcome and 
reclaim one’s power over emotions experienced (David, 2022-b, para. 11). 
Similarly, Lisa Feldman Barrett, author, neuroscientist and Northeastern University 
distinguished professor of psychology is recognized for her study of emotion and expertise in 
affective neuroscience, psychology of emotion, and social and personality psychology. In her 
TED Talk (Barrett, 2018), she suggests that we aren’t at the mercy of our emotions as our brains 
create them, shifting the onus back to ourselves alluding to emotional self-management. She 
suggests that our brains are not wired with emotion circuits and that we don’t have the capacity 
to detect emotions; instead, she believes that “emotions are built, and are not built in” (Barrett, 
2018). She describes emotions as predictions constructed by one’s brain, based on past 
experiences, in order for sensemaking and meaning (Barrett, 2018). 
Hence, Barrett (2018) believes predictions are shaped by new knowledge, actions, and 
the past, and are constructed in preparation for life experiences. Consequently, Barrett (2018) 
 
suggests that we create our own emotions and have more control of them than we think. She 
believes that by changing the emotion producing ingredients (new knowledge, actions, past 
experiences) we can transform our emotional lives by teaching our brains how to predict 
differently, becoming architects of our own experiences (Barrett, 2018). 
Barrett (2018) goes further to suggest that the racing of one’s mind is an example of a 
brain's search for an explanation, or prediction, of bodily sensations experienced in hopes to 
determine next steps. She forces one to question the origin of the sensation, determining whether 
these sensations are purely physical or have transformed into physical discomfort (Barrett, 2018). 
She concludes that given that we are not at the mercy of our emotions, we are in fact responsible 
for them; not necessarily because we are to blame, rather, because we are the only ones who can 
address the emotion (Barrett, 2018). So, if we are to become an emotionally agile society, we 
also need to master individual self-awareness in order to begin to recognize emotional and 
behavioral patterns and work towards effective change. It is important to note that unsuccessful 
emotion regulation can also create a sense of powerlessness (Manz et al, 2016, p. 383). Hence, to 
lead effectively, leaders must cultivate a culture of self-awareness and emotional self-leadership2 
(see emotional self-leadership model in exhibit 9). 
Identified as the top leading competency for the future of work, collaboration requires 
both empathy and self-awareness (AceUp, 2022, p. 10). However, as a prerequisite to self-
awareness, listening with an open mind is also key (AceUp, 2022, p. 3). Human-centered 
leadership calls for one to lead compassionately, increase one’s self-awareness, build strong 
relationships, create inclusive teams, and hone communication skills in hopes for effective 
 2 Emotional Self-Leadership: as an expansion to SL, Manz et al (2016) describes it as the self-influence of emotions. It is a “set of prescriptive strategies aimed at increasing individual effectiveness in regulating emotions and shaping emotional experiences in hopes to circumvent emotional labor” (emotional labor is the “inauthentic expression of emotions, which can deplete mental/physical energy and put health/performance at risk through the stress and strain it creates” (Manz et al, 2016)). 
 
influence (AceUp, 2022, p. 7). And while leadership begins with knowing who you are 
(Maxwell, 2011, p. 45), authentic leadership reinforces the need for self-awareness in order to 
align behaviors with personal values (Cunningham et al, 2020, p. 7), and establish a supportive 
culture of trust, openness, and transparency (Liu et al, 2018, p. 222). Despite it all, Eurich (2018, 
para. 13-15) warns that a false and overconfident sense of self-knowledge can also arise as a 
leader gains more power, overestimating their capacity due to a lack of candid feedback. Self-
awareness is key to accurately discern one’s capacity to avoid experiencing the Dunning-Kruger 
effect3 which reduces one’s opportunity for growth and development (Psychology Today Staff, 
n.d., para. 1). 
Recognized as the Father of Leadership, Warren Bennis perceives leadership as a matter 
of character and as a process of becoming an integrated human being (Gini & Green, 2014, p. 
435). Gini & Green (2014, p. 436) believe that leadership is a lived process that can’t be reduced 
to an algorithm and requires balance and effectiveness, which can only be gained through self-
awareness. Character development in the lens of Plato’s examined life also alludes to the need 
for an understanding of “who you are (your character4) and what you’re willing, or unwilling, to 
do (your integrity and conscience)” (Gini & Green, 2014, p. 438); UCLA basketball coach, John 
Wooden said it best: “the true test of one’s character is what one does when no one is looking” 
(Wright & Lauer, 2013, p. 25). While self-awareness and reflection are critical components of 
adaptability (De Smet, Kothari, & Lavoie, 2021, p. 7), experiences shape a leader's crucibles 
which also require deep self-reflection and life examination (examine values, assumptions, 
 3 Dunning-Kruger Effect: coined by Psychologists David Dunning & Justin Kruger in 1999. It is described as a cognitive bias of wrongly overestimating confidence, knowledge, or ability in an area because of lack of self-awareness (Psychology Today Staff, n.d.) 4 Character Defined: interpenetrable and habitual qualities that constrain and lead one to desire and pursue personal and societal good (Wright & Lauer, 2013). 
 
judgment) (Gini & Green, 2014, p. 441). Gini & Geen (2014, p. 441) believe crucibles are 
transformative experiences in which the basis of one’s identity is shaken. Therefore, emotional 
intelligence is colored by one’s experience, hence, without self-awareness, there is no growth. 
AceUp’s (2022, p. 3) research suggests that there is a disconnect between executives and 
employees, reflecting an unsettling lack of self-awareness as 74% of executives think they’re 
inspiring employees where only 27% of employees agree. And while recognizing the impact of 
career pathing on revenue growth, only 66% of senior leaders stated their organizations had clear 
career paths for all where only 35% of employees agreed (AceUp, 2022, p. 4). The same 
discrepancy exists within retention and cultural strategies, agility capacity, and purpose-driven 
environments (AceUp, 2022, pp. 2-6, ). The question remains, are leaders and organizations 
listening? If power negatively impacts a leader's capacity for empathy (Gratton et al, 2019, p. 4), 
it also hinders their ability for effective self-awareness, collaboration, and impacts their capacity 
to listen, lending to toxic workplace cultures. 
Lingo & McGinn (2020, p. 75) believe that power is “elusive, coveted, enabling, and 
despised” and Azab’s (2020, para. 1) research hints at reasons why. Azab (2020, para. 1) 
suggests that power is “a social lens through which we interact with others, resulting in a 
dependency on the powerful by the powerless.” It negatively influences and damages the brain, 
reducing one’s capacity for empathy and the effective judgment of emotions (Azab, 2020, para. 
5). Azab (2020, para. 5) suggests that the brain of a powerful leader resembles that of a 
psychopath, whose deformity due to frontal brain damage, also impacts their capacity for 
openness to the perspectives of others. Azab (2020, para. 7) believes that “human brains have 
mirror neural networks that are activated when observing the actions of others (activates similar 
brain areas; ie.: a passenger pressing invisible brakes in a car), which are absent in those under 
 
the influence of power; in other words, power desensitizes, hence has the capacity to 
dehumanize. 
This absence results in reduced interpersonal sensitivity, establishing a new mindset that 
hinders connection and relationship building (Azab, 2020, para. 8). Power shifts one’s 
organizational lens from an ecosystem of influence, alignment, empowerment, and partnership to 
an ego-centric system where control, power struggles, self-interest, and territoriality reign. As a 
result, power negatively impacts a leader's capacity to: 1) lead empathetically with compassion; 
2) care, be vulnerable, and emotionally agile; and 3) consciously be aware and embody kindness, 
mindfulness, and love. It requires great courage to lead with care and to create moments that will 
matter long after one’s existence. 
Great leadership is about walking beside; it is not one who is insecure or easily 
threatened, or undermines talent to try to guard their position (Maxwell, 2011, pp. 56-57). 
Maxwell (2011, p. 45) believes that “most obstacles that limit people’s potential are rooted in a 
leader's own fears, ego, and unproductive habits.” And when leaders value their position over 
their ability to influence, workplace environments become political, territorial, and hyper-
focused on control and entitlement, inciting others to do the same (Maxwell, 2011, pp. 53-55). 
Psychological safety demands for leaders to be positively infectious, requiring heightened levels 
of emotional self-awareness and mindfulness (De Smet, 2020, p. 5). Hence, toxic environments 
and power negatively impact and diminish one’s capacity for courage and development. 
Communication as a Leadership Approach 
Leadership communication is recognized as a conduit for influence (message 
transmission and agenda setting), as a tool for sensemaking (leverage language to construct 
reality and meaning - framing), and as a means for dialogue (Cunningham et al, 2020, p. 8). 
 
Cunningham et al (2020, p. 23), believe that there is an interconnection between leadership and 
communication studies in that they both require intentional behaviors for effectiveness. 
Thompson (2013, p. 14) further suggests that “leadership and communication are synonymous” 
as he views effective leadership as a byproduct of effective communication. Essential to high-
performing teams and organizations, Thompson (2013, p. 14) believes that one auditions for 
leadership every time one speaks, and that the quality of one’s communication is indicative of 
the quality of the leader. To that end, effective leadership communication requires contextual 
intelligence to recognize shifts, leverage opportunities, and adapt. 
Influenced by cultural norms, communication is a great tool for increasing awareness, 
engagement, and mobilization, leveraging emotional leadership (pathos) to establish and 
maintain connections (Cunningham et al, 2020, pp. 13-20). Drucker (2004) believes that 
“organizations are held together by information” as communication strategies impact the 
dissemination of information across organizations. In that same vein, de Vries et al (2009, p. 
369) believe that a leader's communication style5 (interpersonal communicative behaviors) is 
driven by their leadership style, and gravely impacts communication behaviors. Consequently, 
one’s communication style will either add-to or detract-from one’s capacity for knowledge 
sharing, collaboration, connection, and followership. Furthermore, one’s communication 
capacity affects organizational effectiveness via positive employee-organization relationships, 
directly impacting employee trust, commitment, and workplace satisfaction (Kim et al, 2022, p. 
2). 
Leading authentically allows room to foster positive climates, cultures, and psychological 
 5 (7) leadership communication styles: de Vries et al (2009) describe them as: expressiveness, preciseness (2nd most important), niceness, supportiveness (most important), verbal aggressiveness, (expressed) emotional tension or opposite assuredness, and argumentativeness. 
 
safety conducive to empowering, open, and vulnerable conversations. Effective organizational 
communication, via authentic leadership, results in “greater self-awareness and self-regulated 
behaviors” (Kim et al, 2022, p. 7). Hence, leaders who develop an understanding of themselves 
and their environments simultaneously develop the capacity for effective leadership 
communication; “leaders who understand…can explain” (Fairhurst, 2005, p. 168). Rubin & 
Carmichael (2018, pp. 57-58) suggest that authenticity (truth) withstands transparency (how 
much you share) and that people define an organization's brand. 
However, while trust is dependent on one’s authentic nature, individual and 
organizational characters also lend shape to cultural environments. Rubin & Carmichael (2018, 
p. 107) define organizational character as “the sum of an organization's beliefs, vision, values, 
words, and actions,” all reputation driving factors. They further suggest that an “organization is 
understood and manifested through four vectors (products and services, environments, 
communications, and behavior) that strategically define how an organization projects its culture, 
vision, and values” (Rubin & Carmichael, 2018, p. 111), providing further evidence that 
effective leadership communication requires a keen sense of self to confront realities. 
When considering leadership as a means for communication, a “failure in communication 
can lead to a failure in leadership as to lead is to communicate” (Ruben & Gigliotti, 2016, p. 
469). Ruben & Gigliotti (2016, pp. 475-476) believe that leadership effectiveness, via a 
reflective practice (self-’guided’ leadership theory), is derived by a collaborative and negotiated 
act (fair value-exchange) between leader and follower with an intended goal of shared meaning. 
Ziek (2014, pp. 317-319) proposes leadership communication as a competency 
(expertise/proficiency in crafting communicative actions) focused on effectively designing 
communication to shape interactions with stakeholders. Through this lens, Beer (2020, p. 34) 
 
believes that organizational transformations are unsuccessful when a leader lacks ample courage 
to transparently address matters, selectively avoiding making the necessary changes in fear of the 
potential impact. Beer (2020, p. 37) believes that a lack of courage stifles a leader's capacity to 
effectively execute strategies due to organizational barriers he has coined as “silent killers6.” 
Furthermore, Wood et al (2023, p. 7) believe that organizational transformation capacity is 
dependent on its people to continuously transform their mindsets, behaviors, and skills. Derkach 
et al (2023, pp. 4-5) further propose five mindset and behavior shifts required for effective 
transformation; shifting to creating impact, co-creation, collaboration, evolution, and authentic 
human leadership. Hence, courageous leadership is underpinned by honest conversations and the 
willingness to be vulnerable. 
As the Professor of Practice at the University of Bath, Margaret Heffernan challenges one 
to dare to disagree. In her TED Talk (Heffernan, 2012), she suggests that openness alone will not 
suffice to drive change. Heffernan (2012) challenges one to see “conflict as constructive thinking 
allowing room for diverse and creative thoughts gained through having thinking partners, as 
opposed to experiencing echo chambers.” She believes that organizations don’t maximize their 
people due to fearful conflict avoidance preferences (unprepared to manage argument, fear of 
appearing unintelligent, or initiating a losing battle). Consequently, she believes that 
organizations don’t know how to effectively think together (Heffernan, 2012). And while, for 
some, challenging leaders and unethical situations may appear to border whistleblowing, 
Heffernan (2012) believes the fear of silence will eventually become louder particularly when 
one is committed to values and purpose. She concludes by suggesting that “the truth won’t set 
 6 Silent Killers of Strategy Execution: “1) Unclear strategy and values, and conflicting priorities; 2) an ineffective senior team; 3) a leader who is top-down or hands-off in order to avoid conflict; 4) a siloed organization that prevents coordination and collaboration; 5) inadequate leadership development and consequently too few down-the-line leaders; 6) no safe organizational mechanisms for lower levels to speak truth to power” (Beer, 2020).  
 
you free until you are able to develop the skills, habit, talent, and moral courage to leverage it; 
she views openness “not as an end, but only as the beginning” (Heffernan, 2012). Leveraging 
courage, self-awareness, and effective communication to lead oneself enables others to also 
elevate and become the best version of themselves. 
Leadership Begins with You 
Leveraging Self-Leadership as a Self-Influence Process and Self-Regulation Tool 
Goleman (2007) suggests that we are wired by default to be compassionate and to 
automatically empathize, however, we continue to witness unsympathetic and indifferent 
behaviors in service and exchange-oriented environments. Many want change but refuse to grow, 
which begs us to question, what impedes one from doing so? At a first glance, one may think it is 
a values, beliefs, or behavior based stance, a matter of timing, a goal misalignment, lack of 
interest, commitment, or simply burnout. However, Eurich (2018, para. 1) alludes to the notion 
that sometimes a refusal to grow may simply be due to mere unawareness. And while 
unawareness may not always be the culprit, one must problem solve with an open mind 
identifying biases and differences between the unaware versus the unapologetically aware. It is 
said that what one ‘looks for’, is what one ‘sees’ and that what one ‘sees’ is influenced by how 
one ‘feels’; however, this stance minimizes vivid and real lived life experiences. Whether 
perceived as internal or external manifestations, self-leadership forces one to take an honest 
inventory, holding oneself accountable and responsible for action. 
Coined by Charles Manz in 1983, the concept of self-leadership is viewed as an 
 
expansion of self-management7 grounded in the theory of self-control8, giving rise to a 
leadership alternative (Neck & Houghton, 2006, p. 270). Integral to the self-management 
process, the concept was applied within the concepts of self-managing teams and the 
empowerment of leadership (aka SuperLeadership9), and was later expanded (late 1990s) to 
include Thought Self-Leadership (Neck & Houghton, 2006, p. 273). 
Neck & Houghton (2006, p. 271) define self-leadership as a “self-influence process 
through which individuals control their own behavior, influencing and leading themselves 
through the use of specific sets of behavioral (self-direction) and cognitive (self-motivation) 
strategies.” They describe self-leadership as a “normative model (prescribe how something 
should be done or show how; see exhibit 10) of self-influence operating within the framework of 
descriptive and deductive theories (describe how and seek to explain; ie.: self-regulation and 
social cognitive theory10) (Neck & Houghton, 2006, p. 275). Neck & Houghton (2006, p. 279) 
allude to three types of self-influence that impact goals and performance: 1) self-satisfaction, 2) 
self-efficacy11, and 3) internal standard regulation. As a normative concept, it “operates within 
the theoretical contexts of self-regulation, social cognitive, self-control, and intrinsic motivation 
theories” (Neck & Houghton, 2006, p. 275). 
 7 Self-Management: “a set of strategies that aides employees in structuring their work environment, establishing self-motivation, and facilitates behaviors for achieving minimal deviations from lower-level behavioral standards” (Manz, C.C., 1986). 8 Self-Control: originally designed for clinical use to manage addictive or self-destructive health-related behaviors. It was later coined self-management for application within organizational contexts. Consists of self- observation/goal-setting/cueing/reinforcement/punishment and rehearsal (Neck & Houghton, 2006). 9 SuperLeadership: as an alternative to Heroic Leadership (heroism and leadership intertwined suggesting transformational leaders are heroes), SuperLeadership is a leadership style developed by Charles Manz which describes a leader as “one who leads others, to lead themselves,” in essence, one who creates self-leaders (Neck & Houghton, 2006). 10 Social Cognitive Theory: explains human behavior via the relationships among internal/external influences and behavior leveraging self-regulatory components - self-monitoring/judgment/reaction (Neck & Houghton, 2006). The social cognitive theory focuses on self-satisfaction/efficacy, whereas self-regulation focuses on internal standards. Focuses on interaction between thoughts, behavior, and social environments. 11 Self-Efficacy Defined: construct within social cognitive theory that describes one’s self-assessment of required capabilities for success, influencing aspirations, efforts, persistence and thought patterns; can be impacted by self-talk and unawareness (primary self-leadership mechanism for performance) (Neck & Houghton, 2006). 
 
Designed to enhance personal effectiveness, self-leadership strategies operate within the 
theoretical framework of self-regulation (Neck & Houghton, 2006, p. 275). They are based on 
self-control and self-management (long term focus) strategies and are grouped into three 
categories (see exhibit 11): 1) behavior-focused (heightens awareness to facilitate behavioral 
management), 2) natural reward (create feelings of competence and self-determination12), and 3) 
constructive thought patterns (creates a way of thinking) (Neck & Houghton, 2006, p. 271). 
Behavioral self-regulation provides a standard for behavior in which behaviors can be 
cognitively adjusted and reevaluated, with the assistance of goals, to shape behaviors (Neck & 
Houghton, 2006, p. 276). Therefore, by way of cognitive strategies, self-leadership influences 
behavioral outcomes (Neck & Houghton, 2006, p. 281). 
Conceptualized as a learned behavior, self-leadership is also positively associated with 
various personality traits such as: “emotional stability (agility), conscientiousness, self-efficacy, 
internal locus of control, and self-monitoring, as well as the Myers-Briggs traits of extraversion, 
sensing, and judging” (Neck & Houghton, 2006, p. 282). Successful self-leadership outcomes are 
dependent on “commitment, independence, creativity, innovation, trust, team potency, positive 
affect, job satisfaction, psychological empowerment, and self-efficacy” (Neck & Houghton, 
2006, p. 283). As a contingent theory, effective self-leadership practices require trust, 
psychological safety, and hence courage. The self-regulation theory suggests that “individuals 
have the tendency to distort feedback received to what they want to see or hear. And when faced 
with difficulty, those who are confident or hopeful tend to persist and even increase efforts made, 
while those who lack confidence or hope search for alternative goals or disengage” (residual 
 12 Self-Determination: mutual reciprocity between motivation and purpose. The self-determination theory (SDT) is the study of human motivation and personality and suggests that successful outcomes are dependent on one’s autonomy, competence, and relatedness, and are required for one’s well-being. 
 
sense13) (Neck & Houghton, 2006, p. 278). Self-awareness is required to confront beliefs and 
assumptions (truths) and leads to more effective self-regulation. Hence, confidence and hope, as 
key components of the self-regulation theory, as well as self-leadership strategies, are 
instrumental in encouraging positive behaviors and addressing hindering mindsets. 
Maxwell (2011, pp. 44, 71) believes that “those who do the most harm, think they have 
arrived thus stop growing, innovating, improving, lowering expectations for themselves and 
others.” Similar to an invitation to the leadership table, and as a component to self-leadership, 
self-awareness is an invitation to personal growth. To be effective, one must be adaptable, 
curious, open minded, agile, and have a desire to continually develop in hopes to increase one’s 
leadership sphere of influence (Maxwell, 2011, p. 44). Recognizing that employees tend to 
conform to norms established by leaders, the development of one’s self-awareness along with the 
Pygmalion effect phenomenon14, (aka Rosenthal effect or self-fulfilling prophecy15) can be 
positively leveraged to cultivate the adoption of a growth and development mindset to shape 
behaviors (Maidenberg, 2021, para. 8). 
Shaping Trajectories via Behavioral Design 
As change agents, how do leaders effectively pave paths and drive long-term and 
 13 Residual Sense Defined: turn automatically to previously encoded sources of information about expectations when facing problems or difficulties; when challenged, one turns to old habits; habitual way of thinking (thought patterns) (Neck & Houghton, 2006). 14 Pygmalion Effect Defined: a behavioral science principle that suggests that other-imposed (type of self-fulfilling prophecy) beliefs or expectations influence one's behaviors or outcomes (Maidenberg, 2021). Also known as the self-fulfilling prophecy, or Rosenthal effect, it was coined by Psychologists Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson in the 1960s (Maidenberg, 2021). It originated from the Greek poem, Metamorphoses, written by Ovid, a Latin poet from Rome, in which Pygmalion (a sculptor) is enamored with a statue and asks the Gods to bring her to life as his wife; his request is answered and the statue comes to life.  15 Self-fulfilling Prophecy Defined: coined in 1948 by Sociologist Robert K. Merton describes “a false definition of the situation, evoking a behavior which makes the originally false conception come true” (Schaedig, 2023). There are two types of prophecies: self- (one’s expectations influence one’s behaviors) and other-imposed (others’ expectations influence your behaviors). Hence is a prediction that causes itself to become true, consciously or subconsciously, through action or inaction (Schaedig, 2023). Our actions impact others beliefs that cause other actions toward us reinforcing our own beliefs. 
 
sustainable change to address workplace challenges? It takes courage to empathetically pause 
and identify areas requiring change. However, as an initial step, courage alone is not enough to 
shift towards impactful change. I recently had the opportunity to meet with Gina Soloperto, a 
behavior design research and strategy specialist, who suggested that “we all want change, but 
change is hard.” Her expertise in the study of people, has led her to believe that “understanding 
environments at the basic human level of fight, flight, or freeze responses are key.” She strongly 
believes that “it is imperative for leaders to understand the value of human relationships and 
engagement as leading is relationship based.” 
Soloperto suggests that “stigmas (negative or unfair beliefs) generally derive from a lack 
of understanding or knowing”; in this lens, unawareness can then be perceived as a state that 
heightens a self-perpetuating stunted growth and development process. Consequently, she 
suggests “leveraging a framework built on three pillars: 1) contextual factors (how one gets 
things done; includes organizational cultures and climates, psychological environments and self-
limiting beliefs), 2) mindsets (motivations, beliefs, fears, heuristics, and emotions that trigger 
emotional responses), and 3) emotions (impacts decision making) to inform decision making and 
drive desired responses or behaviors.” In essence, Soloperto suggests that context (stimulus) + 
mindsets & emotions (thinking) = drive behaviors (response). 
Soloperto suggests that “effective behavior (response) change can only result when 
specific, measurable (Key Performance Indicators (KPI) tied back to behaviors) desired behavior 
changes are identified and tied back to organizational values and goals, resulting in greater 
engagement and reduced attrition rates.” As the founder of the behavior design movement (see 
exhibit 12 for behavior model), BJ Fogg suggests that “motivation, ability, and a prompt must 
converge at the same moment for a behavior to occur” (Fogg, n.d., para. 1). Soloperto believes 
 
that “low motivation/low ability (competency) can lead one to question whether the task is too 
difficult or whether the individual is right for the team. Whereas, when one is highly motivated, 
but has low ability, one tends to find a way to get a task done.” 
Similar to Fogg’s behavior model, Soloperto leverages the three pillars (which 
simultaneously occur during decision making) for effective behavior design, which also aligns 
with the three basic human needs (1. relatedness: desire to connect and feel understood; 2. 
competency: am I absorbing info, do I understand, can I do it; and 3. autonomy: have knowledge 
& skills to know what one’s doing) identified via the self-determination theory (SDT). In line 
with Fogg’s concept (motivation vs ability model), Soloperto leverages a control vs support 
model (Job Demand-Control-Support (JDCS) model) to predict behaviors. She believes that 
“effective behavior change must be built into bite size action steps in order to break down 
complex and ambiguous outcomes, connected back to personal values aligned to shared 
organizational values, vision, and purpose.” She believes that “habits are formed out of repeated 
behaviors, thus developing new habits requires courage to build one’s competency levels to 
increase one’s skills, awareness, and understanding; thereby positively impacting one’s 
autonomy.” 
Soloperto suggests that “courage is hidden in the (SDT) process and one’s psychological 
needs and derives from a lack of competency or relatedness.” She believes that “courage is 
embedded in intrinsic (one’s purpose/calling/belief in practice) and extrinsic (something you are 
incentivized or have to do) motivation, and that extrinsic motivators, specifically, must be 
connected to a larger goal to make them doable.” Her perspective is also aligned with Neck & 
Houghton (2006, p. 272) as they believe “natural reward strategies are designed to create feelings 
of competence and self-determination (primary mechanisms of intrinsic motivation) lending to 
 
performance-enhancing task-related behaviors.” She further suggests that the “effect of power vs 
powerlessness stems from a disconnect from the top-down, whereby knowledge gained from the 
support received (via executive coaching, BoD advisory support, etc.) is not cascading outside of 
the top of the house; thus, recommends the placement of agile coaches within individual teams 
for appropriate dissemination.” 
Lastly, Soloperto believes that “workplace accountability is lost as leaders are saying the 
right things, but are not doing them.” She believes “it is not just about behavior change for 
outcomes, but leading also requires cultivating cultures that enable people to be their best selves, 
ensuring that they feel seen and heard.” With a marketing, design, and project management lens, 
Soloperto views “management as an opportunity for human development and as a process that 
moves people through systems in structured uniform ways for alignment.” This lens reinforces 
the notion that everything starts or ends with leadership (Maxwell, 2007, p. 267). 
Bridging the concepts of self-determination, self-leadership, and behavior change models, 
Neck & Houghton (2006, p. 285) believe “self-leadership may enhance feelings of empowerment 
by creating perceptions of meaningfulness, purpose, self-determination, and competence. As 
such, effective self-leadership and development can be viewed as a continual process and 
lifelong journey dependent on a growth mindset as beliefs and values drive behaviors. This 
research suggests that courage, self-awareness, and communication are positively correlated with 
one’s development capacity as it requires an open mind to vulnerably, and deeply, self-reflect to 
reveal, understand, and manifest one's beliefs and values via effective communication and self-
regulated behaviors. Hence, courage requires action (self-determination) to stimulate the 
necessary motivation to become self-aware, and lean towards positive behavior change. 
 
 
Leading towards a Self-Leadership-Culture (SLC) 
Self-Leadership Culture (SLC) Defined: 
“A self-leadership culture is one where individuals strive toward leading one’s own life in a 
free and independent manner. They act in accordance with their inner values and beliefs, 
bearing the development of a larger socio-organizational entity in mind, and using effective 
self-leadership strategies for goal attainment. Leaders are seen as facilitators of these 
behaviors, namely authenticity, intrapreneurship, and self-leadership” (Bracht et al, 2018, 
p. 125). 
A self-leadership culture (SLC) hones in on elements of leadership-culture that 
specifically impact assumptions (beliefs) and behavioral norms within an organizational culture 
(Bracht et al, 2018, pp. 122-123). Bracht et al (2018, p. 122) believe that a SLC can shape group 
norms, and when combined with the Social Identity Theory of Leadership (SITL)16, it creates a 
sense of belonging, increasing one’s well-being. They suggest that “leadership towards self-
leadership is instrumental to tapping into intelligence, creativity, commitment, and individual 
potential and can assist to understand individual and team success” (Bracht et al, 2018, p. 119). 
According to Bracht et al (2018, p. 122), organizational cultures consist of underlying 
assumptions (about humans; level 1: idea of man17), beliefs (subconscious beliefs that guide 
behavior) and values (based on past experiences; level 2: leadership philosophy18), and artifacts 
(level 3: visible, audible, or touchable materializations- ie.: dress code; office design, etc.), 
hence, view leadership-culture as an element of organizational culture. These three levels 
(ranging from top to bottom) depict human assumptions, how we think about and design 
 16 SITL Defined: Individual’s knowledge that he [or she] belongs to certain social groups together with some emotional and value significance (Bracht et al, 2018). 17 Idea of Man: Notion that human beings possess the necessary abilities, self-discipline, and self-control to lead themselves (Bracht et al, 2018). 18 Leadership Philosophy: refers to the way we think about and design collaboration and leadership based on beliefs and values that influence leader-follower interaction. 
 
leadership strategies, and the artifacts that are a result of the norms set, based on assumptions 
made. As a form of authentic behavior, SLC proposes alignment with one’s values to increase 
one’s performance, leveraging the three self-leadership strategies for organizational goal 
attainment (Bracht et al, 2018, p. 123). This alternative perspective shifts the traditional lens of 
leadership from influencing others to perform to influencing oneself towards performance 
(Bracht et al, 2018, p. 120). 
With the fear that self-focus would negatively impact a group's performance, Bracht et al 
(2018, p. 120) suggest three extensions of the self-leadership concept. First, they suggest the 
concept of intrapreneurship (entrepreneur within an existing organization) as an expression of 
individual employee behaviors toward the larger socio-organizational entity, actively 
contributing to an organization in a decentralized fashion (Bracht et al, 2018, pp. 120-121). 
Second, they suggest that a self-leader has the capacity to authentically change their own 
attitudes, values, beliefs, and behaviors to achieve personal goals (Bracht et al, 2018, p. 121). 
Therefore, in the context of authentic leadership, self-leaders leverage self-goal setting to 
enhance consistency between their beliefs and actions, where their own prescribed values 
become the basis for motivation and change (Bracht et al, 2018, p. 121). Lastly, with an 
organizational lens, and as a proposed solution for competitiveness, they suggest that self-
leadership enables employees to successfully lead themselves towards organizational outcomes 
(Bracht et al, 2018, p. 121). 
Drawing from servant leadership and SuperLeadership, Bracht et al (2018, p. 125) 
believe that a SLC positively influences leader-member exchange (LMX19) relationships as it 
 19 Leader-Member Exchange Theory: refers to the dyadic relationship between leader and follower (Bracht et al, 2018). It is a relationship-based leadership theory viewed as a shared activity that impacts the quality of leader-member experiences. Hence, no two relationships will be one and the same (ie.: a leader can be perceived/experienced differently by separate team members or direct reports). 
 
encourages empowerment and support. A SLC suggests self-leading as a force-multiplying 
framework conducive for changing behaviors, shifting the focus from organizational to internal 
transformation (Bracht et al, 2018, p. 120). The proposed culture of individual self-management 
makes sense to the extent that actions based on authentic values can increase job satisfaction, 
knowledge sharing, and employee motivation towards change for the greater good (Bracht et al, 
2018, p. 125). And, while encouraging self-leadership, it also encourages one to do so within 
context, particularly within personal vs professional self-leadership. As a spin to Maslow’s 
motivational theory, a SLC encourages motivation from within based on one’s own beliefs and 
values. Leveraging the concept of SLC, a culture of self-leadership can encourage proactive 
behaviors with an eye towards development and growth, particularly with organizational 
outcomes in mind. However, in contrast to SuperLeadership (lead others, to lead yourself), self-
leadership suggests for one to become a transformational self-leader (lead self, to lead others), 
embodying the changes one wishes to see. 
Connecting the Dots 
Organizational transformation begins with individual self-transformation achieved via 
effective behavioral, natural reward, and constructive thought self-leadership strategies. As an 
expansion of self-management, (grounded in self-control and operating within the theoretical 
concepts of self-regulation, social-cognitive, and intrinsic motivation theories), self-leading, via 
self-awareness, is foundational before one can teach or lead. Self-leadership shapes behaviors 
and can enable, or disable, effective communication and self-expression thus an honest revealing 
of self requires emotional agility to create a positive impact. Consequently, it is one’s 
responsibility to cultivate one's desired environment and self-lead, humbly serving with an 
attitude of gratitude. Despite obtaining a seat at the table, leadership is an opportunity that 
 
actively requires one to, daily, choose to lead. 
Leaders set the tone and direction of organizations, hence a listening campaign is only 
effective when organizations are actively listening for the sake of leaning towards positive 
impact, climates (employee experiences), and cultures (based on values, beliefs, assumptions). 
Despite the culprit or whether aware or unaware, leaders are called to take action and continue 
moving an organization towards its identified mark. And while employee movements may 
appear similar to a revolving door and way of life, organizational cultures depict unspoken truths 
identifying areas of much needed change. Organizational cultures drip towards, and play a 
pivotal role in, performance, engagement, revenue growth, retention, and turnover and are a 
direct reflection of leadership capacity. If circumstances and statistics aren’t improving, are 
organizations listening or merely driving agendas? Leadership is a choice that calls for 
responsibility, impact, and action which is not an easy feat as to whom much is given, much is 
required. 
Foundational to human values, courage is the key to human-centered and inclusive 
leadership as courageous leaders lead from a heart stance. Communications and behaviors 
impact how organizations are perceived, impacting trust, commitment, transformational capacity, 
job satisfaction, and more importantly, one’s capacity to lead. Fostering safe cultures is 
dependent on trust, effective communication, self-awareness, and courage to encourage positive 
behaviors and confront hindering mindsets as without self-awareness, there is no self-
development. 
Consequently, considering courage, self-awareness, and communication separately will 
not suffice to shift towards or drive impactful change. Leveraging all three to lead oneself, 
however, enables others to do the same as courage drives self-awareness, self-awareness lends to 
 
effective communication, and communication is the glue and conduit for courageous self-
awareness. As such, leading, effective relationship building, and driving connections require one 
to, first, connect with oneself (Maxwell, 2011, pp 105). Leveraging one’s moral courage and 
daring to disagree, as suggested by Heffernan (2012), will result in greater self-awareness and 
self-regulated behaviors achieved via the process of self-influence. Elevating truth found within 
self-awareness to set one free, via courageous and effective communication, will position leaders 
and organizations for transformative experiences and greater impact. 
As a leadership competency designed to shape interactions, effective leadership 
communication is an expression of language and thought in hopes for shared meaning as “leaders 
cannot not communicate” (Drucker, 2004). One’s communication capacity directly impacts 
organizational effectiveness and communicative behaviors affecting employee-organization 
relationships. Crucial for relationship building, trust assists one to lead through uncertainty and 
effectively influence (also self-influence) and serve, positively impacting goals and performance. 
Effective communication is key for communicative dynamics as it shapes and guides a leader's 
capacity to influence, highlighting the power of framing to shape narratives and shift towards a 
solution orientation. 
Self-leadership assists with interpersonal conflict resolution when aligned with one’s 
values. Clarifying one’s purpose, practicing emotional awareness, establishing a positive 
outlook, asking quality questions, seeking feedback, and practicing self-reflection can assist to 
increase one’s self-leadership capacity (Gambill, 2022). Self-leadership requires a level of 
awareness to understand oneself (one’s emotions and impact) impacting decision making, 
problem solving, and collaboration. As such, self-leadership encourages a continual evolution of 
individual perspectives, framing and reframing experiences for personal success. 
 
Similar to Heffernan (2012), I believe one has more control than one thinks to self-lead, 
particularly when practicing self-leadership strategies to work towards a desired end and regulate 
thoughts, behaviors, and social environments. Leveraging self-determination as a driver for self-
leadership behaviors can assist the development of one’s capacity. Perceived as behavioral 
facilitators, leaders assist to shape and guide organizational norms affording them the 
opportunity to proactively foster future and emerging leaders. And while leadership capacities 
can be developed, leaders are called to lead by example and self-lead in hopes to effectively lead 
others. 
For those who still argue that emotions don’t have a place at work, the relationship 
between authentic leadership, subordinate behaviors, and psychological ramifications need to be 
further considered as organizations continue to struggle with implementing mindful behaviors 
within relationship-based organizations. With the behavior change equation in mind (context (S) 
+ mindsets & emotions (T) = drive behaviors (R)), further research should explore the 
relationship between courage (3 elements: emotional, cognitive, and behavioral), negative 
emotions, such as stress and anger, and self-development relative to disengagement to better 
understand how one can assist with ongoing workplace challenges. 
Cultivating a self-leadership culture is a force-multiplying framework conducive for 
behavior change. It encourages and enhances leader-member dynamics towards empowered 
individual performance and successful organizational outcomes. Self-leadership reframed is self-
awareness as it leads to the transformation of self. All of our experiences lead us on a journey 
where every step brings us closer to who we are and where we should be. Before one can present 
their best self, safe cultures must be cultivated. Self-leadership-cultures demand for all to rise 
and cultivate safe environments by leading oneself accordingly. Leading is not solely the 
 
responsibility of leaders or HR as it is said that between stimulus and response there is a space. 
That space is a choice for learning conducive to growth and development, allowing room for one 
to create a personal culture of continual becoming to positively guide behaviors and drive results. 
So, to effectively lead others, lead yourself first, from within!

Characteristic: Description: 
Intellectual Courage 
Consists of intellectual (IK) and emotional (EK) knowledge. IK provides an understanding of what to do, how to do it, and why. Whereas EK provides an understanding of why things are being done. 
Moral Courage Moral values are the main sources of human decisions, behaviors, and actions and are leveraged: for honesty and integrity; to distinguish right from wrong, do the right things, seek justice, take responsibility, fulfill commitments, possess humility, show respect and serve, stand up for what is right, and encourage/develop others. 
Creativity Courage 
Process of finding new ways to make radical changes and solve difficult problems, including paradigm shifts (radical/destructive change of entire organization). The birthing of NEW. Know the past, see the present, and predict the future. 
Biological Courage 
Inherited personal courage obtained through learning, doing, and training that provides competitive advantages for understanding, thinking, and analyzing. 
Followers Courage 
Necessary courage for effective leadership practices. Followers should be independent critical thinkers, active participators, engage beyond scope of role, have sense of ownership, problem solve, make decisions, have awareness of self and others, have the will to accept responsibility, take risks to challenge authority, and participate in change.

 iii 
Abstract 
This study examined a social exchange approach to influencing employee attitudes, behavior, and performance. Social exchange theory predicts that employees will respond, in kind, to the treatment they receive from the organization. It was proposed, therefore, that organizations can influence the attitudes, behavior, and performance of employees by attending to the relationships that develop between employees and the organization. This study examined the relationships between leader-member exchange, organizational citizenship behavior, and perceived organizational support. 
Surveys were administered to 49 employees and their supervisors at three separate country clubs located in the southwestern United States. Perceptions of organizational support, leader-member exchange, and organizational citizenship behavior were assessed. Mean scores, standard deviations, analysis of variance, and Spearman’s correlations were calculated to measure the constructs and determine possible relationships. 
Overall, employees reported that they believed they received some support from the organization and some support from their manager. Employees’ altruistic and general compliance behaviors were rated favorably by their supervisors. Analysis of variance calculations suggested that these variables did not vary by age, gender, education, or tenure. 
The research aimed to answer three questions: Does leader-member exchange have a positive relationship on organizational citizenship behavior? Does perceived organizational support have a positive relationship with organizational citizenship behavior? Does leader-member exchange have a stronger relationship to organizational citizenship behavior than perceived organization support to organizational citizenship behavior? The results showed a positive, statistically significant relationship between general compliance and altruism (from the organizational citizenship behavior survey) and between perceived organizational support and leader-member exchange. These results suggest that as altruism increases, general compliance also increases (and vice versa). Similarly, as perceived organizational support increases, leader-member exchange also tends to increase (and vice versa). No other relationships among the variables could be concluded. 
Limitations of this study are its small sample, the applicability of organizational citizenship behavior to a hospitality setting, the limitations of quantitative research for complex topics, and the natural conflict between customer service and organizational citizenship behavior.
